meta.title: The Editor's Desk
meta.subtitle: Meridian Press, 1953–1997
meta.course: Cambridge International AS & A Level History 9489 · Paper 3 · The origins and development of the Cold War

scoring.notes: Main argument, concession, school and approach count towards Scholarly Integrity; the stamp counts towards Board Compliance only. For the concession, any sentence listed in key.concessions is correct; if the list is empty, the correct answer is 'No concession'. If the correct school is 'not_blame' and the player picks it, the approach step is skipped and its point awarded; if the player wrongly picks 'not_blame', the approach step is skipped and its point lost.

traditionalist.label: Traditionalist (orthodox)
traditionalist.definition: Blames the Soviet Union. Soviet expansion in Eastern Europe, driven by communist ideology or an appetite for power, caused the conflict; the USA responded defensively.

dissenting.label: Dissenting
dissenting.definition: Places the main blame on US policy, for example a 'get tough' approach, atomic diplomacy, or ignoring Soviet security needs. (In 1953 these critics were a minority; their ideas later fed into revisionism.)

revisionist.label: Revisionist
revisionist.definition: Shifts the blame onto the USA, usually through American economic aims (open markets, the dollar, the Marshall Plan) and sometimes atomic diplomacy. Soviet actions are often seen as defensive reactions.

post_revisionist.label: Post-revisionist
post_revisionist.definition: Attaches blame to both sides (often for different things), or to neither, explaining the conflict through the post-war situation such as the power vacuum and mutual insecurity. The extract must actually argue this; it is not simply 'nobody's fault'.

post_post_revisionist.label: Post-post-revisionist
post_post_revisionist.definition: The 'new' Cold War history written since the Soviet archives began to open after 1991. Gives prime responsibility to Stalin, stressing his ideology and personality. It can look like traditionalism, but the USA is not simply vindicated.

not_blame.label: Not an argument about blame
not_blame.definition: Discusses Cold War events without making a case about what caused the conflict.

days.title: The Committee Is Watching
days.climate: The Red Scare is at its height. A congressional Committee on Publications is reviewing what American presses print.
days.directive: The Committee on Publications reminds Meridian Press that responsible scholarship recognises Soviet responsibility for the present world crisis. Publish only manuscripts that place responsibility for the Cold War on the Soviet Union. Reject all others.
days.rulebookTip: Judge the argument, not the tone. An author can sound anti-communist and still blame Washington.

days.title: A New Generation
days.climate: The war in Vietnam has divided the country. Young scholars are questioning the official story of American foreign policy.
days.directive: The board wants Meridian at the forefront of the new critical scholarship. Publish only manuscripts that place the main responsibility for the Cold War on the United States. Reject all others.
days.rulebookTip: Many authors open by admitting the other side's best point. Read on: where does the argument end up?

days.title: Détente
days.climate: The superpowers are talking again. Newly declassified records from the 1940s are reaching the libraries.
days.directive: In the spirit of détente, the board wants balanced scholarship. Publish only post-revisionist manuscripts. Reject any manuscript that places the main responsibility on one superpower.
days.rulebookTip: 'Both sides' or 'neither side' must be argued by the extract. Words like 'misunderstanding' are not enough on their own.

days.title: The Archives Open
days.climate: The Soviet Union has collapsed and its archives are partly open. Historians are testing old arguments against new evidence.
days.directive: The board wants Meridian to publish the new Cold War history. Publish only post-post-revisionist manuscripts. Reject all others. From today, some manuscripts arrive anonymised, as extracts do in the exam: judge the extract alone.
days.rulebookTip: Using Soviet archives does not make an extract post-post-revisionist. Some Russian historians have used the same archives to argue that Soviet aims were more limited and defensive. Ask: who is blamed, and for what?

traps.concession: Concession trap: the author admits a point from the other side, then turns it back. Classifying from the concession gets it wrong.
traps.tone: Tone trap: the author's tone or opening sentence points one way, but the argument points the other.
traps.dossier: Misleading dossier: the author's background points one way, but the extract points the other. The extract always wins.
traps.subject: Subject trap: the extract mentions Cold War events but makes no case about what caused the Cold War.
traps.half_reading: Half-reading trap: the first sentences point to one school, but the extract goes on to blame the other side too.
traps.misunderstanding_label: Label trap: the extract mentions misunderstanding, but it does not argue that both sides were to blame. It blames one side.
traps.archives: Archives trap: the extract uses Soviet archives, but that does not make it post-post-revisionist. Check who it blames.
traps.trad_vs_ppr: Traditionalist or post-post-revisionist? Both blame the USSR. Look for whether the USA is simply vindicated, and whether the blame rests on Stalin's personality or ideology using new evidence.
traps.neither_valid: Valid 'neither side': unlike a vague 'misunderstanding' claim, this extract argues why the situation itself produced conflict.

dossier.name: Dr Walter Prentiss
dossier.role: Associate Professor of International Relations, Brookfield College
sources: State Department reports on Eastern Europe
Dispatches from US missions in Bucharest and Sofia

sentences: In the summer of 1945 the victorious allies still spoke of a common peace.
Yet in Romania a Soviet envoy had already forced the King to appoint a communist-led government, only weeks after the Yalta promise of free elections.
In Hungary and Bulgaria, opposition parties were broken up one by one.
These were not accidents of occupation: the Soviet Union broke the wartime understanding, using the Red Army to extend its rule as far into Europe as it could reach.
Washington protested, but it did not act until the Truman Doctrine of 1947, and then only to halt Soviet pressure on Greece and Turkey.
Even then, the United States offered Marshall aid to East and West alike.
manuscripts.explanation: Sentence 4 states the argument: the Soviet Union broke the wartime understanding by using the Red Army to extend its rule. Sentences 2–3 give the evidence, and sentences 5–6 cast the USA as slow to respond and still open-handed. The West is not criticised anywhere, so there is no concession.
anchors: Yalta Conference and the Declaration on Liberated Europe (February 1945)

dossier.name: Dr Margaret Ellery
dossier.role: Lecturer in Modern History, Harwell University
sources: Memoirs of American and British wartime diplomats
Records of the foreign ministers' conferences, 1945–47

sentences: Critics of American policy are fond of listing its mistakes, and some of their charges are fair.
Washington was slow to explain its aims, and its talk of an 'open door' in Eastern Europe must have sounded to Moscow like interference.
But misjudgements of tone do not start a cold war.
The conflict came because the Soviet leadership believed, as a matter of doctrine, that no lasting peace with capitalist states was possible.
In February 1946 Stalin told Soviet voters that capitalism inevitably bred war, and Soviet policy behaved accordingly.
Every Western offer of cooperation was read in Moscow as a trick, and every agreement as a pause before the next advance.
manuscripts.explanation: Sentences 1–2 concede American mistakes, but sentence 3 dismisses them as 'misjudgements of tone'. Sentence 4 states the argument: Soviet doctrine made lasting peace impossible, supported by Stalin's 1946 speech (sentence 5).
anchors: American 'open door' policy and Eastern Europe (1945–46)

dossier.name: Dr Samuel Orrin
dossier.role: Professor of Political Science, a Midwestern state university
sources: Published records of the Yalta and Potsdam conferences

sentences: Communism is a cruel creed, and nothing written here should be read as a defence of it.
Yet the historian's question is not whether the Soviet system was admirable but why the wartime alliance broke apart.
The answer lies chiefly in Washington, where a new administration refused to accept that the Soviet Union had legitimate security needs in Eastern Europe.
When the Soviet foreign minister called at the White House in April 1945, the new President lectured him as though he were a junior official.
It is true that Soviet conduct in Poland gave Washington genuine cause for complaint.
But a country invaded through Poland twice in thirty years could not be expected to accept a hostile government there, and American leaders refused to see it.
manuscripts.explanation: The anti-communist opening (sentence 1) is not the argument. Sentence 3 places the blame on Washington for ignoring Soviet security needs, illustrated by Truman's treatment of Molotov (sentence 4). Sentence 5 concedes Soviet misconduct in Poland, but sentence 6 explains it as a security need.

dossier.name: Mr Peter Hallam
dossier.role: Former economic officer, US Office of Military Government in Germany

sentences: The Soviet blockade of Berlin has made the currency reform of June 1948 famous for the wrong reason.
The reform certainly provoked Moscow, and the Russians treated it as a political challenge.
Its real importance lay elsewhere: it was the single measure that restarted the West German economy.
Before the reform, goods vanished from the shops because no one would sell for worthless Reichsmarks, and cigarettes served as money.
Within weeks of the new Deutschmark, shop windows filled and factory output rose sharply.
Planners elsewhere should study how a sound currency, more than any loan, can revive a broken economy.
manuscripts.explanation: Sentence 1 mentions the blockade and sentence 2 concedes the reform's political impact, but sentence 3 states a different argument: the reform mattered because it revived the West German economy. The extract makes no case about what caused the Cold War.

dossier.name: Dr Rose Kettering
dossier.role: Instructor in History, a New York college; campaigned for Henry Wallace's Progressive Party in 1948

sentences: Like many on the American left, I once believed that a little more generosity from Washington would have kept the peace.
The record of the past eight years has changed my mind.
I still think American diplomats were often clumsy, and that the sudden end of Lend-Lease in 1945 was handled badly.
But clumsiness answered by clumsiness is the stuff of ordinary diplomacy; it does not explain the Cold War.
What explains it is Stalin himself: a ruler so suspicious that he treated every independent government on his borders as a threat and every Western concession as weakness.
His treatment of Mikołajczyk, driven out of Poland in 1947, and of Tito, expelled from the communist bloc in 1948, shows the same pattern.
No American policy, however wise, could have satisfied such a man.
manuscripts.explanation: The dossier suggests a Wallace supporter, and sentence 3 concedes American clumsiness, but sentence 4 dismisses it as ordinary diplomacy. Sentence 5 places the blame on Stalin's suspicious personality, illustrated in sentence 6.

dossier.name: Dr Carl Hendry
dossier.role: Associate Professor of History, a Midwestern state university
sources: Records of the Bretton Woods conference

sentences: The orthodox story begins in Warsaw and Bucharest, with Soviet tanks and rigged elections.
Those events were real, and no honest account can excuse them.
But the story begins earlier, in the planning rooms of Washington, where officials were determined that the post-war world would be open to American trade.
It was this determination, rather than any Soviet plan of conquest, that turned an awkward alliance into a Cold War.
At Bretton Woods in 1944 the United States built a world economy around the dollar, and in 1945 it offered a large loan to Britain while a Soviet request for reconstruction credit went unanswered.
A closed Soviet sphere in Eastern Europe threatened that design, and so it had to be resisted.
Soviet repression in the region followed American pressure; it did not cause it.
manuscripts.explanation: Sentences 1–2 concede the Soviet record in Eastern Europe, but sentence 3 moves the story to Washington. Sentence 4 states the argument: the American determination to keep the world open to US trade caused the Cold War, supported by Bretton Woods and loan diplomacy (sentence 5).
anchors: Soviet request for a US reconstruction loan (1945)

dossier.name: Dr Nina Galloway
dossier.role: Research Fellow, a Washington institute for policy studies
sources: Papers of the Joint Chiefs of Staff

sentences: Stalin was no innocent, and Soviet behaviour in 1945 gave Americans real reasons for unease.
Yet the papers of the Joint Chiefs of Staff show how far American planning had moved beyond defence.
By the end of the war the United States held the atomic bomb, the world's largest navy and a chain of air bases stretching from Iceland to the Pacific.
American planners wanted to keep all three, and to add bases closer to Soviet borders.
This drive to turn wartime victory into permanent global supremacy, not Soviet aggression, set the superpowers on the road to the Cold War.
Seen from Moscow, a ring of American bases looked less like defence than encirclement, and Soviet hostility grew accordingly.
Moscow, admittedly, did little to explain its own intentions, but a weaker power can hardly be blamed for caution.
manuscripts.explanation: Sentence 1 concedes Soviet faults and sentence 7 concedes Soviet secrecy, but neither carries the argument. Sentence 5 blames the American drive for global supremacy, shown through the atomic monopoly and the network of overseas bases (sentences 3–4).
anchors: US military planning for overseas bases (1943–46)

dossier.name: Dr Alan Whitlow
dossier.role: Assistant Professor of History, a California state college; co-founder of a campus committee against the Vietnam War
sources: Reports of the US embassy in Tehran

sentences: The war in Vietnam has taught my generation to distrust official explanations, and rightly so.
But distrust is not a method, and on the origins of the Cold War the official story is closer to the truth than its new critics allow.
In 1946 Soviet troops stayed in northern Iran after the date agreed for their withdrawal, while Moscow pressed Tehran for an oil concession.
That summer the Soviet government demanded a share in the defence of the Turkish Straits, a demand Turkey rightly took as a threat.
American policy was sometimes heavy-handed, and the language of the Truman Doctrine was certainly overblown.
Yet these crises show a Soviet state probing for weakness wherever it could, and it was this expansion that turned rivalry into a Cold War.
Where the West stood firm, as in Iran and Turkey, Moscow drew back; where it did not, as in Eastern Europe, Soviet power advanced.
manuscripts.explanation: The anti-war dossier and the opening sentence suggest a critic of American policy, and sentence 5 concedes American heavy-handedness. But sentence 6 blames Soviet expansion, shown in the Iran and Turkish Straits crises (sentences 3–4).

dossier.name: Dr Grace Fennimore
dossier.role: Lecturer in Politics, a Scottish university

sentences: Many now argue that the Truman Doctrine of March 1947 committed the United States to a needless global crusade against communism.
There is something in this, and the sweeping language of the speech did outrun the modest aid it requested for Greece and Turkey.
But this study asks a narrower question: how did a cautious, economy-minded Congress come to vote the money at all?
The answer lies in domestic politics: Truman needed the votes of Republicans who wanted lower taxes, and alarming rhetoric was the price of their support.
Senator Vandenberg, the leading Republican on foreign affairs, reportedly advised the President to 'scare hell out of the American people'.
The speech did exactly that, and the aid bill passed both houses by large majorities within two months.
manuscripts.explanation: Sentence 1 sounds like a revisionist charge and sentence 2 partly concedes it, but sentence 3 sets out a different question. Sentence 4 argues about how Congress was persuaded to pass the aid, not about what caused the Cold War.

dossier.name: Dr Ethan Morrow
dossier.role: Assistant Professor, a New England college
sources: US military government records from Germany
Speeches of Secretary of State Byrnes
Minutes of the Allied Control Council

sentences: In May 1946 the American military governor in Germany halted reparations deliveries from the US zone to the Soviet Union.
Four months later, at Stuttgart, Secretary of State Byrnes promised the Germans that the United States would help them rebuild.
Soviet officials, it must be said, had stripped their own zone of factories with little regard for the German population, and their complaints were not always made in good faith.
Even so, the meaning of American policy was plain in Moscow: the country that had invaded the Soviet Union twice in thirty years was to be revived as an American partner.
By choosing the recovery of western Germany over Soviet security, the United States made the division of Germany, and of Europe, unavoidable.
The merging of the British and American zones in January 1947 was only the first step.
Every later Soviet move in Germany, the Berlin blockade included, was a reaction to a decision already taken in Washington.
manuscripts.explanation: Sentences 1–2 set out American decisions on Germany. Sentence 3 concedes Soviet asset-stripping and bad faith, but sentence 4 turns to Soviet fear of a revived Germany. Sentence 5 states the argument: putting German recovery before Soviet security made division unavoidable.
anchors: US halts reparations from its zone (May 1946)

dossier.name: Dr Laura Benning
dossier.role: Professor of Diplomatic History, a Pennsylvania university

sentences: When Moscow rejected Marshall aid in July 1947 and forced its neighbours to do the same, it divided Europe.
The founding of the Cominform that September, with its talk of two hostile camps, confirmed the division in the language of class war.
Yet the American side of the story, now visible in declassified records, is less innocent than it once appeared.
Washington framed the Marshall Plan so that Soviet participation would be difficult, and many officials privately hoped Moscow would refuse.
The Cold War in Europe was therefore a joint creation: each side took steps it believed defensive, and each treated the other's steps as proof of hostility.
It is true that Soviet methods in Eastern Europe were far harsher than anything the United States did in the West.
But harshness is not the same as sole responsibility, and neither government was willing to accept the risks that cooperation would have required.
manuscripts.explanation: Sentences 1–2 read as traditionalist, but sentence 3 turns to American responsibility, shown in sentence 4. Sentence 5 states the argument: the Cold War was a joint creation of mutual insecurity. Sentence 6 concedes that Soviet methods were harsher, but sentence 7 refuses to make that sole responsibility.

dossier.name: Dr Henry Okafor
dossier.role: Senior Lecturer in International History, a London university
sources: Records of the Paris conference on Marshall aid, 1947

sentences: Recent writers like to call the breakdown of 1947 a tragedy of misunderstanding, in which each superpower misread the other's defensive aims.
It is fair to say that Moscow often misread Western motives, and that Soviet suspicion made every negotiation harder.
But the Americans who designed the Marshall Plan misunderstood nothing.
They knew that its conditions, an open account of each country's resources and joint planning under American oversight, were ones Moscow would never accept.
The division of Europe was not a misunderstanding but the intended price of an American economic strategy that put open markets before agreement with Moscow.
When Molotov walked out of the Paris conference in July 1947, Washington's planners were relieved rather than surprised.
Misunderstanding is a comfortable word for a choice.
manuscripts.explanation: The 'misunderstanding' language in sentences 1–2 is a concession. Sentence 3 says the Americans misunderstood nothing, and sentence 5 places the blame on an American economic strategy that accepted a divided Europe.

dossier.name: Dr Daniel Ashby
dossier.role: Research Fellow in Asian Studies, an Australian university
sources: Records of the US occupation of Korea

sentences: Both superpowers bear some responsibility for the tragedy of Korea, and both later used the peninsula for their own purposes.
This essay, however, asks a narrower question: how was the dividing line itself chosen?
The 38th parallel was not the product of a long-laid plan by either side but a hurried improvisation by junior officers in Washington.
On the night of 10–11 August 1945, two American colonels, working from a small wall map, picked the parallel because it left the capital, Seoul, in the American zone.
The Soviet command accepted the line without objection, and its forces halted there as agreed.
No one involved expected a temporary military boundary to become a frontier between two hostile states.
manuscripts.explanation: Sentence 1 sounds post-revisionist, but sentence 2 sets out a different question. Sentence 3 argues that the 38th parallel was a hurried improvisation: the extract explains how Korea was divided, not what caused the Cold War. It makes no concession.
anchors: Division of Korea at the 38th parallel (August 1945)
Soviet and American occupation of Korea (August–September 1945)

dossier.name: Dr Robert Vance
dossier.role: Professor of History, a Texas university
sources: Published Soviet and East German documents

sentences: Post-revisionist scholars have shown that American leaders made mistakes in 1945 and 1946, and that some suspicion between the victors was inevitable.
They are right, too, that Washington sometimes spoke more harshly than it acted.
But balance becomes a fault when the evidence points one way.
In the Soviet zone of Germany, the occupying power forced the Social Democrats to merge with the Communists in April 1946, creating a party that answered to Moscow.
In Czechoslovakia, the last coalition government in Eastern Europe fell to a communist coup in February 1948.
Wherever the Red Army stood, Soviet power was extended by force, and it was this steady expansion, not American mistakes, that turned post-war rivalry into a Cold War.
The West's response, from the Marshall Plan to NATO, came only after these advances.
manuscripts.explanation: Sentences 1–2 concede post-revisionist points, but sentence 3 rejects balance. Sentences 4–5 give evidence of Soviet expansion, and sentence 6 states the argument: Soviet expansion, not American mistakes, caused the Cold War.

dossier.name: Dr Annika Lund
dossier.role: Research Fellow, a Stockholm institute of international affairs
sources: Diplomatic records of several European states

sentences: The Cold War was the product of the situation in 1945, not the guilt of either side.
Historians have spent thirty years trying to decide which capital started it, as if a different choice in Moscow or Washington would have kept the peace.
With Germany and Japan defeated and Britain exhausted, only two powers were left to fill the vacuum in Europe and Asia.
Each had good reason to fear the other, since each had the strength to threaten what the other most valued.
Neither leadership was blameless, and both made choices that sharpened the conflict.
Yet even wiser leaders would have faced the same clash of interests over Germany, the one prize neither could allow the other to win.
manuscripts.explanation: This 'neither side' argument is earned: sentence 1 places the cause in the post-war situation, and sentences 3–4 explain the power vacuum and mutual fear. Sentence 5 concedes mistakes on both sides, but sentence 6 argues that the clash over Germany would have happened anyway.

dossier.name: Dr Thomas Ridley
dossier.role: Professor of International History, a US research university
sources: Records of Stalin's meetings with foreign communist leaders

sentences: American leaders were not saints, and the new archives do nothing to rescue Truman's crude diplomacy in 1945.
Nor do they reveal a Soviet master plan for world conquest; Stalin was cautious and often improvised.
What the archives do show is a ruler whose suspicion poisoned every relationship he touched.
It was Stalin's personality, more than any system or situation, that made the Cold War.
Records of his meetings with foreign communists show him demanding obedience on the smallest matters and treating any sign of independence as betrayal.
When Tito resisted, Stalin had Yugoslavia expelled from the Cominform in 1948.
A leader who could not trust his own allies was never going to trust his capitalist rivals.
manuscripts.explanation: Sentences 1–2 concede points to revisionists and post-revisionists, and the USA is not vindicated. Sentence 4 states the argument: Stalin's personality made the Cold War, supported by new archival evidence of his suspicion (sentences 5–6).
anchors: Expulsion of Yugoslavia from the Cominform (June 1948)

dossier.name: [Redacted]
dossier.role: [Redacted]

sentences: The United States entered the post-war world wanting nothing more than to bring its soldiers home.
Its rapid demobilisation, its offer of Marshall aid to East and West alike, and its proposal to place atomic energy under international control all show a nation seeking peace.
Admittedly, some American officials spoke with needless harshness.
But from the Baltic to the Balkans, Soviet occupation was followed by communist rule.
Pressure on Iran, Turkey and Greece showed that Soviet ambitions did not stop at the edge of Eastern Europe.
The Cold War was therefore the result of one power's appetite for territory, and the free world was forced to respond.
NATO, founded in 1949, was the free world's reluctant answer.
manuscripts.explanation: This blames the USSR in the traditional way. The USA is fully vindicated as peace-seeking (sentences 1–2), the blame falls on the Soviet state's appetite for territory (sentence 6) rather than Stalin's personality or ideology, and no new evidence is used. Sentence 3's concession is brushed aside.
anchors: Baruch Plan for international control of atomic energy (June 1946)

dossier.name: Dr Yelena Sorokina
dossier.role: Senior Researcher, a Moscow institute of general history
sources: Archive of Foreign Policy of the Russian Federation

sentences: Western readers of our archives have found what they expected: a suspicious dictator and a brutal system.
Those findings are accurate, and Stalin's treatment of Eastern Europe cannot be defended.
But the same archives show that the Soviet delegation came to the Paris conference on Marshall aid in June 1947 instructed to explore participation, not to wreck it.
Moscow withdrew only when it concluded that the conditions would open its sphere to Western control.
The Cold War in Europe arose from this collision of two security systems, each defensive in its own eyes, and the evidence does not support placing the burden on Moscow alone.
Washington wanted an open Europe it could rebuild; Moscow wanted a closed buffer it could trust.
Neither aim was unreasonable, and neither could be achieved without defeating the other.
manuscripts.explanation: This uses the Soviet archives but does not blame Stalin. Sentence 2 concedes Stalin's brutality, but sentences 3–4 show Soviet caution over Marshall aid. Sentence 5 states the argument: a collision of two defensive security systems, with the blame shared. This is a Russian perspective, not post-post-revisionism.

dossier.name: [Redacted]
dossier.role: [Redacted]

sentences: Stalin's foreign policy was often cautious, and in 1945 he did not want a war with the West.
He told communists in France and Italy not to seize power, and for years he hoped for a united, neutral Germany.
Yet evidence from the Soviet archives shows that it was his Marxist-Leninist ideology that made a Cold War certain.
He expected the capitalist powers to quarrel among themselves and the Americans to leave Europe, so he saw no need to compromise.
When the Western powers drew together instead, he concluded that they were preparing to attack, and he tightened his grip on Eastern Europe.
The Berlin blockade of 1948 was the gamble of a man who believed history was on his side, and its failure only deepened his suspicion.
manuscripts.explanation: Sentences 1–2 concede Stalin's caution. Sentence 3 turns to new Soviet evidence and states the argument: Stalin's Marxist-Leninist ideology made the Cold War certain, shown in his expectations and reactions (sentences 4–6). The USA is not simply vindicated.
anchors: Stalin's advice to French and Italian communists (1944–45)

dossier.name: [Redacted]
dossier.role: [Redacted]

sentences: The opening of the Soviet archives has encouraged a wave of books that place the blame squarely on Stalin.
Nobody now doubts that the Soviet leader was a tyrant, or that his regime did terrible things in Eastern Europe.
But tyranny inside the Soviet bloc does not explain why Europe was divided, and on that question the American archives matter more.
In May 1947 Under Secretary of State William Clayton warned that a collapse in Europe would close markets on which the American economy depended.
The Marshall Plan turned that fear into policy, and its conditions were drafted in the expectation that Moscow would refuse them.
The Cold War grew out of this American determination to rebuild Europe as an open, dollar-based market, a goal that left no room for a Soviet sphere.
manuscripts.explanation: The extract mentions the Soviet archives and Stalin's tyranny (sentences 1–2), but sentence 3 sets them aside. American economic aims, shown in Clayton's warning and the Marshall Plan (sentences 4–5), carry the blame in sentence 6.
anchors: Clayton memorandum on the European crisis (May 1947)

integrityBands.text: Your classifications were consistently accurate. You read every manuscript for its argument, not its tone or its author.
Mostly accurate. Check the end-of-day reviews for the traps that caught you.
You were often led by concessions or dossiers. Practise finding the sentence where the argument turns.
The traps won this time. Replay and focus on the final sentence of each extract.

endings.twoAxisNote: Board Compliance shows how well you obeyed each era's political pressure. Scholarly Integrity shows how accurately you read the historians. Only integrity measures your skill as a historian.

summary: 1950s: Orthodox (traditionalist) accounts dominated, in a climate of anti-communism that made dissent costly.
1960s: Revisionism grew as the Vietnam War led many to question American foreign policy, and American economic aims came under scrutiny.
1970s: Post-revisionism emerged during détente, as newly declassified Western records encouraged more balanced accounts.

1990s: The opening of Soviet archives produced post-post-revisionism, which returned the focus to Stalin's ideology and personality, while some Russian historians used the same records to reach different conclusions.
debrief.reflectionPrompt: Why might the time and place in which a historian writes affect who they blame for the Cold War?
debrief.examReminder: In the exam the author and date are not given. You must identify the interpretation and approach from the extract alone, as on Day 4.
